objectives: Explain what a token is and why models work in tokens instead of letters.
Describe how text becomes tokens and back again.
Estimate how many tokens a piece of text uses.
Explain what a context window limits and what happens when it fills.
Write a prompt that gives a model the context it needs.
Recognise when a long conversation has become unreliable and start a fresh one.
Explain the cost of a message in practical terms.

sections.body:
A token is the unit of text that a language model actually reads and writes. It is not a word, and it is not a character. It is a chunk, usually somewhere between a character and a word, chosen so that the most common pieces of text can be stored efficiently.

The word "unbelievable" might be split into a few tokens. The word "the" is usually one token. A space is often attached to the next word, so " the" is one token, not two. This means the same sentence can cost more or less depending on the words in it, and it means that text in a language with different word shapes costs differently from English.

The reason for tokens is arithmetic. A model turns text into numbers and then works on those numbers. The unit has to be big enough that the vocabulary stays manageable, and small enough that the sequence does not become enormous. Roughly speaking, **one token is about four characters of English**, or about three quarters of a word. A page of English prose is around 500 to 700 tokens.

Everything else follows from this. The **context window** is the number of tokens a model can hold at once: your message, the conversation so far, any document you uploaded, and the instructions it was given. When the conversation grows past that limit, the oldest parts are pushed out. The model does not forget because it is distracted. It forgets because the tokens are literally not there any more.

This single fact explains most of the strange behaviour people notice. A chatbot that seems to have lost the plot halfway through a long chat has usually not lost it; the beginning has been pushed out of the window. A chatbot that cannot read your 40-page PDF has not refused; the file is larger than the window. A chatbot that contradicts itself has two different token sequences to work from, and it answered the one in front of it.

And a final point that matters commercially: tokens are also the unit of billing. When a provider quotes a price per token, they are telling you what it costs to feed text in and get text out. Understanding tokens turns an opaque price into a quantity you can measure.
examples: The document was not too difficult. It was 90,000 tokens, and the window is 8,000.
It did not get confused. The first part of our chat had already left the window.
sections.heading: What a token is, and why everything is measured in them

sections.body:
Every message goes through the same four steps. Knowing them turns a strange result into a diagnosable one.

**Step one, tokenisation.** Your text is split into tokens by a tokenizer, a fixed vocabulary built for the model. This is mechanical, and it is where the cost is calculated.

**Step two, embedding.** Each token is turned into a list of numbers, a vector, that captures what the piece of text means in relation to every other piece. Tokens with similar meaning sit close together in that space. "Bank" the financial institution and "bank" the river end up in different places.

**Step three, prediction.** The model runs through the whole sequence at once, layer by layer, and works out what should come next. It is doing this for every position in parallel, which is why it can handle thousands of tokens at once and why it does not read your text the way you read a page.

**Step four, decoding.** The chosen tokens are turned back into text and sent to you. If you asked for a shorter answer or a different format, that instruction is itself part of the input sequence, and the model tries to honour it the same way it tries to honour everything else.

Two consequences follow from this pipeline. The first is that **the model has no memory outside the window**. There is no hidden store of your conversation. When a service says it remembers you, that memory lives in a database on their side and is pasted back in as part of the input.

The second is that **instructions compete with content**. Everything you send occupies the same budget: the system instructions, the chat history, your documents, and your question. When a service runs out of room, it drops something, and it does not always drop the thing you would have chosen.
examples: Every message becomes tokens, then numbers, then a prediction, then text again.
The model has no memory of our chat except what is in the window right now.
The system instructions take the same room as my question, and the room is finite.
sections.heading: What happens between your message and the answer

sections.body:
You rarely need an exact count. You need to know roughly whether a piece of text will fit, and the rough rules are simple enough to carry in your head.

**Rule one: divide the character count by four.** A message of 4,000 English characters is around 1,000 tokens. This works well for ordinary prose, because English averages a little under four characters per token.

**Rule two: count words, then add a third.** A word is roughly 1.3 tokens, because spaces and common word endings become their own tokens. A 300-word email is roughly 400 tokens.

**Rule three: expect other languages and formats to cost more.** Vietnamese text with its multi-syllable words and full diacritics tends to tokenise less efficiently than English. Tables, code, and JSON are dense with symbols, and symbols are often their own tokens. A spreadsheet pasted in may cost several times what its word count suggests.

**Rule four: the input and the output are counted separately.** Asking for a long answer costs you twice: once for reading your prompt, once for generating the reply. A request for a 2,000-word answer costs about 2,600 output tokens, plus whatever the prompt used.

These rules are enough for daily decisions. When a task is genuinely near the limit, most interfaces show a token count or a progress indicator, and some let you see the budget. Use those rather than estimating when the exact number matters, because a single pasted table can move the count by thousands.

One habit saves trouble: put the instruction first and the material second. If a document is long, ask the model to process it in named parts and give you a short summary of each. You keep the summary, you keep the parts, and the parts stay inside the window.
examples: Rough rule: 4,000 characters is about 1,000 tokens, so I need to cut the document in three.
A 300-word email is roughly 400 tokens, and the reply will be about the same again.
I asked for one section at a time, and each answer stayed inside the window.
sections.heading: How to estimate the token count of a message

sections.body:
The context window is the model's working memory for a single conversation. It is measured in tokens and it is the hardest limit in the whole system, because it decides what the model can possibly know while answering you.

Windows range widely. A small model might hold a few thousand tokens. A current general assistant might hold tens of thousands, and some tools hold hundreds of thousands or more. A million tokens is roughly the length of a long novel, which sounds generous until you remember that the window must hold your question, the reply, any uploaded files, and the system instructions at the same time.

When the window fills, something has to go. Most commonly the system drops the oldest turns of the conversation. Sometimes it summarises them and keeps the summary. Either way the model now answers with a slightly wrong version of the past, and it has no way to tell you that the past is incomplete.

The symptoms are recognisable. The model starts forgetting an instruction you gave at the beginning. It begins contradicting a fact it established twenty turns ago. It loses the file you uploaded. It begins repeating itself near the end. In all four cases, the cause is usually the same, and none of them is a failure of the model itself.

A long conversation feels like progress because it contains a lot of work. Inside the model, it is just a long token sequence, and past a certain size the early part is gone. Two habits follow. After every few useful turns, ask for a short summary in a fixed format: decisions, open questions, facts to keep, and the current task. Then start the next chat with that summary pasted in at the top. It costs a minute and buys you a clean context.

The practical fix is therefore to **start a fresh conversation and carry a summary forward**. This feels wasteful, because you have invested twenty turns. It is cheaper than the alternative, because you are otherwise paying for a long context in which your early material is invisible.

The other practical fix is to **keep the working set small**. Ask for short answers, ask for numbered lists, ask it to tell you which part of the document it used. When the context stays small, the quality of the answer usually rises, not falls.
examples: Let us start a new chat. I will paste a summary of where we got to.
It forgot the format I asked for at the start, because that was pushed out long ago.
I keep the working set small now: one document, one question, short answers.
sections.heading: The context window, and what happens when it fills

sections.body:
A prompt is the text that becomes the first part of the context window. It is worth two minutes of thought, because everything you leave out is budget you keep for the answer.

First, put the task in the first sentence. The model reads the whole window, but a clear instruction at the top is the one least likely to be drowned out.

Second, state the audience and the format. "Explain to a new warehouse supervisor" and "give me five bullet points" remove most of the guesswork, and they remove the need for a long back-and-forth that would eat the window.

Third, give the constraints you would otherwise be asked for: length, tone, language, what to do when the information is missing.

Fourth, put the long material after the instruction, and mark it clearly. Bracketing the source material makes it obvious what is data and what is a request, which reduces the risk of the model treating a sentence inside your document as an instruction.

Fifth, ask for the reasoning you need when you need it, not always. A request to show the steps costs tokens and can add confident mistakes. A request for a short answer with the assumption stated is often better.

Sixth, and last, ask the model to say what it does not know. It is cheap, and it turns a confident guess into a visible gap.
examples: Here is a document in square brackets. Answer only from it, and say when it does not answer.
Explain for a new warehouse supervisor, in five bullet points, under 150 words.
Give me the short answer first, then the reasoning, and mark anything you had to assume.
sections.heading: How to write a prompt that uses the window well
steps: Put the task in the first sentence.
State the audience, the format and the length.
Give the constraints you would otherwise be asked for.
Place long source material after the instruction, clearly marked.
Ask for reasoning only where you need to check it.
Ask what it is unsure about, and treat that as part of the answer.

sections.body:
These are the terms you meet in model documentation, in pricing pages and in developer discussions.

**Token** is the chunk of text a model reads or writes, usually a word, a part of a word, or a common symbol.

**Tokenizer** is the fixed list of tokens a model uses, and the rule that turns text into them and back.

**Context window** is the maximum number of tokens the model can hold at once, counting the question, the history, the documents and the instructions together.

**Prompt** is the instruction and context you give the model. It becomes the first tokens of the sequence.

**Completion** is what the model produces. On older terminology, the prompt is the input and the completion is the output.

**Input tokens** and **output tokens** are the two sides of the bill. Prices are quoted for each.

**System prompt** is the standing instruction that sets the behaviour of the assistant, the tone, the limits. It is a token cost like any other.

**Temperature** is the setting that controls how much randomness the model uses when choosing the next token. Low values give repetitive answers, high values give varied and less reliable ones.

**Truncation** is what happens when the input is longer than the window: the excess is cut, usually from the oldest part.

**Context drift** is the gradual change in a model's answers over a long conversation, as the working context fills with old material and pushes out the original instructions.

sections.body:
Prices are quoted per token, and that hides more than it shows. Two models can cost very different amounts for the same task, because the price per token, the number of tokens your text produces, and the number of tokens the answer takes all vary.

The practical comparison is the **cost of the task**, not the price per token. A cheap model that needs four attempts because its answers were unusable is more expensive than a pricier model that works first time. A model that reads a 50,000-token document every time you ask a question is expensive in a way that a model reading a 2,000-token summary is not.

Three habits keep the cost predictable. **Summarise once, reuse many times.** Paste the long document once, get a structured summary, and work from the summary. **Keep the history short.** Every previous turn is input tokens you pay for again in every message. **Ask for the length you need.** Output tokens are billed per token, so "in five bullet points" is a real instruction with a real price.

There is a cost to careless pasting too. Sending a large document with personal data in it costs money, puts that data in someone else's system, and takes a long time. Reading the first two paragraphs and pasting those is often both cheaper and better.

One more thing is worth saying plainly: token prices keep falling, and the way people price their own work changes with it. A task that was priced by the hour becomes a task that is priced per use. The skill that matters moves towards deciding what to ask for, how to check it, and when to do it by hand.
examples: I summarised the contract once and now I am working from four pages instead of forty.
It is cheaper to pay for the better model once than to fix the cheap model's answer three times.
I asked for five bullet points because output is billed by the token.
sections.heading: What a token costs, in practice

sections.body: These sentences explain the behaviour people find confusing, and they are useful with a colleague, a teacher, or a support line. Use them as they are, and change the detail to fit your own situation.
examples: It does not read letters. It reads tokens, which are chunks of text.
Four characters is a good rough estimate of one token in English.
The file was too big for the window, so it was truncated, not refused.
Your chat history is not memory. It is context, and it has a size limit.
I keep a summary at the top of a new chat so the window stays useful.
The price is per token, so a long conversation is paid for on every message.
Ask for the format you want in the first sentence, not in the tenth.
sections.heading: Sentences you can reuse when you talk about tokens

sections.body: Most complaints about chatbots are about how the request was framed, not about the model. Four habits recover most of the difference. Put the task first, in one sentence, and say what a good answer looks like. Keep the working set small: one document, one question, one task at a time, and ask for the answer in a short form. Bring context with you when you start a new chat, in a fixed template of decisions, open questions and facts to keep. And check the parts that matter: the numbers, the names, the quotations. A model is fast at producing something plausible and slow at confirming it, so the checking stays with you. These four habits work with every model you will meet, including the ones that arrive next year.
sections.heading: Getting more out of the same model

item.summary: A chatbot does not read your message; it reads tokens, and the limits on how many tokens it can hold explain most of what feels strange about it. After reading this you can explain what a token is, judge whether a message will fit in the context window, count tokens roughly, write prompts that get better answers, and recognise the moment a long chat has stopped being reliable.
